I've been farming these 4 mu of land in Quzhou County for over forty years. This year, like most years here on the North China Plain, I'm sticking with the wheat-maize double-cropping system that works best for our climate and soil. My winter wheat went into the ground last October — I planted an improved variety, Shi 4185, because it handles our dry springs well and gives steady yields. Right now it's the start of April, the wheat is turning green and entering the jointing stage, so I'm getting ready for the first top-dressing of urea and the first irrigation if the rain doesn't come. I figure four irrigations for the wheat this year: green-up, jointing, heading, and grain-filling. I'll spray twice for aphids and fungal diseases.

After I harvest the wheat in early June, I'll immediately plant summer maize — I'm going with a hybrid variety, Zhengdan 958. It's reliable and I can get good grain quality for the market. I'll put down compound fertilizer at planting and top-dress at the big-flare stage. Three irrigations should be enough for the maize if the summer rains cooperate. I'll run the rotary tiller before wheat planting, but for the maize after wheat, I'll likely do minimal tillage to save time and moisture — maybe light rotary tillage just to clear the stubble. I'm educated enough to read the county's extension bulletins, but I'm also old enough to trust what my eyes tell me about the field. I don't chase fancy new seeds anymore; I want proven yield.
